justice: Spatial resources are distributed relatively evenly, with sidewalks on both sides of the street, a central median, and organized carriageway space rather than one side monopolizing the public realm.
The roadside transit stop/shelter and the visible pedestrian warning sign indicate that the corridor serves more than private cars and provides some support for multiple user groups.
Accessibility is moderate rather than excellent because the sidewalks appear continuous and paved, but no curb ramps, tactile paving, or other barrier-free details are clearly visible in the image.
Fairness is supported by the posted 30 km/h speed limit and the no-horn sign, which suggest road rules intended to protect all users rather than prioritizing fast vehicle movement only.
safety: The roadway is wide, well-marked, and lane arrows are clearly painted, which improves predictability for drivers and reduces maneuvering conflicts.
A central guardrail/median barrier separates opposing traffic streams and helps prevent dangerous crossing and head-on conflicts.
The visible 30 km/h speed limit sign and school/pedestrian crossing warning sign indicate traffic-calming intent and attention to vulnerable crossing areas.
Streetlights are installed along the corridor, which likely improves nighttime visibility and personal safety.
Safety is not perfect because the street is broad and crossing distances may still feel long for pedestrians if designated crosswalks are spaced far apart.
livability: The environment appears orderly and clean, with maintained pavement, trimmed median planting, and coordinated street furniture, which supports everyday urban quality.
Mid- and high-rise buildings along the corridor suggest a mixed urban district with nearby destinations and potential residential or institutional activity.
A bus stop or transit information pillar on the right side improves daily mobility options and supports access to services without needing a private car.
Livability is moderated by the relatively low level of visible street life; there are few pedestrians, cyclists, benches, or active storefront edges directly engaging the sidewalk.
sustainability: The presence of a transit stop supports lower-carbon travel by giving an alternative to private car use.
The landscaped median and roadside greenery provide some ecological value and minor heat and air-quality benefits compared with a fully hardscaped street.
The corridor design appears compact and urban, with dense buildings that can support shorter trip distances and more efficient land use.
Sustainability is limited by the dominance of asphalt roadway space and the modest amount of tree canopy, which reduces shade, cooling, and stormwater benefits.
aesthetics: The street has a strong visual order, with consistent light poles, guardrails, paving, and lane markings creating a coherent and well-designed appearance.
The curved roof forms of the low buildings on both sides add architectural character and make the corridor more visually distinctive.
The skyline with tall towers framed by the open sky creates a clear focal point and a pleasing sense of depth.
Clean surfaces, limited clutter, and maintained planting contribute to a polished and attractive streetscape.
comfort: Physical comfort is fairly good because the sidewalks appear smooth, continuous, and separated from moving traffic by curbs and planted strips in some sections.
Psychological comfort benefits from the low apparent traffic volume, organized lane structure, and no-horn regulation, which can reduce stress and noise exposure.
Thermal comfort is weaker because there is little visible tree canopy over the sidewalks or roadway, leaving users exposed to sun and heat during the day.
There are no clearly visible benches or resting amenities, so comfort for waiting or lingering is limited despite the presence of a transit stop.
walkability: Continuous sidewalks are visible on both sides, giving pedestrians a defined place to walk rather than forcing them into the carriageway.
Traffic management features such as the 30 km/h sign, pedestrian warning sign, and separated roadway edges improve the overall walking environment.
The street looks clean, legible, and unobstructed, which supports straightforward pedestrian movement.
Walkability is reduced by the wide road profile and limited visible shade, and no marked crosswalk is clearly seen in the immediate foreground.
bikeability: The smooth pavement and relatively calm, well-regulated traffic environment could make cycling feasible for confident riders.
The broad corridor offers enough width that a bicycle facility could be accommodated, and the street geometry is easy to read.
Bikeability remains limited because no clearly marked or protected bike lane is visible on either side of the roadway.
No bicycle parking, bike symbols, or intersection treatments for cyclists are apparent, so cycling support infrastructure appears incomplete.
